opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think there's actually a really nice parallel there. If you go back to the early days of language models, around 2018 or 2019, the field was quite fragmented. Every lab had its own codebase, its own way of loading a model, its own little tricks, and it was really hard for someone outside those labs to just pick up a model and build on it. A big part of what we did with Transformers was simply to lower that barrier: one library, a common interface, a place to share checkpoints and datasets. Suddenly thousands of people could experiment, and the community did the rest.

When I look at robotics today, it feels a lot like language was back then. You have amazing research, but it's scattered. Datasets are in all kinds of formats, every hardware platform has its own stack, and reproducing a paper often means rebuilding half the system from scratch. So our role is quite similar in spirit. With LeRobot we're trying to build the shared layer: a common format for robot datasets, easy ways to train and evaluate policies, pretrained models people can fine-tune, and a hub where all of that can be shared openly.

There's one big difference, though, and it's the hardware. With language models, everything lives in software. You download weights and you're done. In robotics you need an actual physical robot, and those have traditionally been expensive and closed. That's why we've gotten more involved on the hardware side as well, with low-cost, open-source arms and making them easy to build and buy. If only a handful of well-funded labs can afford robots, you'll never get the kind of community-driven progress we saw in NLP.

So in a way, we see ourselves playing the same role, being the open platform and the connective tissue for the community, but in robotics we have to go a bit deeper down the stack, all the way to the physical world. And honestly, I think the opportunity is huge. Data is the main bottleneck in robotics right now, and an open community collecting and sharing data together could be what really unlocks the field.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the role is actually quite similar in spirit, but the timing is very different, and that changes a lot.

With language models, we arrived somewhat after the fact. The Transformer was there, BERT was there, GPT was there, and what was missing was a place where all of this could be shared, compared, reused. So we built the library, then the Hub, and the community did the rest. We were the infrastructure for a field that was already exploding.

In robotics, we're arriving much earlier in the curve. The field today reminds me a lot of NLP around 2017 or 2018. There are a handful of labs with very good results, but everything is siloed. Every lab has its own robot, its own data format, its own training code, and if you want to reproduce a paper you basically have to rebuild everything from scratch. There's no equivalent of "pip install transformers and load the checkpoint." That's exactly the gap we think we can fill.

So with LeRobot, the idea is to do for robotics what we did for language: standardize datasets so a policy trained on one robot can be shared and fine-tuned on another, make the models open and easy to run, and bring the cost of entry way down. That last part is maybe the biggest difference. In language, the barrier was compute and expertise. In robotics, the barrier is also hardware. If you need a fifty thousand dollar arm to participate, the community stays tiny. That's why we've pushed so much on cheap, open hardware, something you can build for a few hundred dollars and put on your desk. If a student in Lagos or Jakarta can collect data and train a policy on a Friday evening, the field moves at a completely different speed.

The other thing I'd say is that in robotics, open source is not just nice to have, it's probably necessary. Data is the bottleneck, and no single company will collect enough diverse, real-world data on its own. The internet gave us free text. There is no internet of robot trajectories yet. The only realistic way to get there is thousands of people contributing from many different robots and environments, and that only happens if the tools and formats are open and shared.

So in short: same philosophy, democratize the technology, make it reproducible, let the community build on each other's work. But in robotics we get to be there from the beginning, and we have to care about atoms as much as bits.

astra-6.text:
I think the role is quite similar: make it easier for people to build on each other’s work. With language models, we’ve helped bring models, datasets, and tools into a shared ecosystem, so you don’t have to start from scratch every time you have an idea.

In robotics, that’s harder because you have the physical world involved. Different robots have different hardware, collecting data takes effort, and something that works in one environment may fail in another. So sharing a model is only part of the problem. You also need ways to share data, reproduce experiments, and connect the software to the hardware.

For me, the opportunity is to make robotics accessible to a much broader community. We don’t need to build every robot ourselves. We want to help someone take what another team has done, understand it, improve it, and contribute that improvement back.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the role is quite similar: we want to make it easier for people to share their work and build on each other’s progress. With language models, that means models, datasets, and tools that a whole community can use. In robotics, you need those things too, but you also have the physical hardware, which adds another barrier to participation.

So the opportunity is to bring those pieces together—to make robots more accessible, make it easier to collect and share data, and let people reproduce what someone else has done. We don’t need to build every robot or every model ourselves. We want to help create the infrastructure where lots of people can contribute, experiment, and move the field forward together.
